The internal taxes, whatever they might be, their wisest, they did not venture until, without the advice of Mr. Jefferson, to make perpetual. Those taxes were temporary; some of them would have ceased to this day, had not the desire of the party to preserve the trappings of monarchy indulged them to pass the law of the 4th of February 1801, by which they were made permanent. To satisfy the public that the design of the opposition in objecting to the repeal of the internal taxes, was solely to embarrass government and not to relieve the poor, who, while they fret it with moderation, are as much comforted by spirits as by tea or sugar; it is proper to examine their conduct while in power, a little more minutely. Instead of lessening the duties on these articles, at the month of February 1797, when they had the benefit of their knowledge of the operation of the duties for more than six years, they increased them. Every member of congress from Connecticut (including Griswold and Dana), every member from New-Hampshire, and every member present from Massachusetts (excepting Wm. Lyman) voted in favor of that measure. At the same session, a law was passed granting relief to distillers, by removing the duty from the amount of spirits and fixing it on the capacity of the still. Many politicians have adopted a proverb, that the want of news is an indication of the prosperous state of the world; what then must we think of the prosperity of our political affairs, when there is not even a single measure of our general government, which can excite disquiet and discussion, though there is a party in this country, who with all the anxious avidity of the hawk, are continually watching for their prey? No wars, no armies to disgust us by their presence and cast a gloom over our future prospects; no excise gatherers to gauge our stills, to measure our windows, and to excite our indignation; no sedition law to muzzle the press and introduce suspicions into the convivial circle; no proscription. Our government seems to have realized that admirable theory, which the most-enlightened politicians have delighted to contemplate; where the administration is scarcely seen on the theatre of action, and man is left to the undisturbed exercise of his individual energies. Not a solitary basis can be found for even federal cavil or federal denunciation.... Richmond Eng. Congress of the United States. HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES. SATURDAY, Feb. 14. The House proceeded to the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd ballot for President, but the result was invariably 8 for Jefferson, 6 for Burr, two divided. The further balloting was adjourned until Monday, 12 o’clock. A letter from the Secretary of the Treasury was received; but was not read. After the 30th ballot, a motion was made to postpone the next ballot to the 2nd March; which was rejected unanimously by the States. Monday, Feb. 16. The House proceeded to the 34th ballot, The result the same as before. Next ballot postponed until tomorrow, at 12 o’clock, Tuesday, Feb. 17. The House proceeded to the 35th ballot for President. The result the same as before. At one o’clock the 36th ballot was taken, which issued in the election of THOMAS JEFFERSON. After the declaration of the choice, a bill for declaring all letters received by or written to JOHN ADAMS, free of postage, was twice read. On Thursday, July 4th, the Students of the University joined to celebrate the day. A procession was formed at the College and moved thence to the Chapel, where the throne of Grace being addressed by the President, an oration was pronounced by James Brackett, at once eloquent and impressive. The procession then moved to the Booth where the following toasts were drank under the discharge of cannon. 1. The day we celebrate—the birthday of Liberty and Independence; May we testify our readiness to defend its rights, by our enjoyment of its blessings. 2. The United States of America; May party animosities and political contentions soon be floating on that sea, whose waters wash the shores of other worlds. 3. Thomas Jefferson, President of the United States; May his measures be such, as shall advance the honor and happiness of the nation. 4. The State of New-Hampshire; So long as her hills are crowned with verdure so long may her children continue to preserve their political integrity. 5. John Langdon; By measures the most salutary, may he convince his constituents, that wisdom and virtue are the basis of good government. 6. The firm patriots of '76; Ever zealous to defend the rights of their country, and more ready to die freemen, than to live slaves. 7. The political constitution of the United States—firm and unshaken as its founders.

The act of Congress of February 3rd, 1805, for building and employing a number of gun-boats, is now in a course of execution to the extent there provided for. The obstacle to naval enterprise which vessels of this construction offer for our sea-port towns, their utility towards supporting within our waters the authority of the laws, the promptness with which they are manned by the seamen and militia of the place in the moment they are wanting, the facility of their assembling from different parts of the coast to any point where they are required in greater force than ordinary, the economy of their maintenance and preservation from decay when not in actual service, and the competence of our finances to this defensive provision without any new burden, are considerations which will have due weight with Congress in deciding on the expediency of adding to their number from year to year, as experience shall test their utility, until all our important harbours, by these and auxiliary means, shall be secured against insult and opposition to the laws. No circumstance has arisen since your last session which calls for any augmentation of our regular military force. Should any improvement occur in the militia system, that will always be seasonable. Accounts of the receipts and expenditures of the last year, with estimates for the ensuing one, will, as usual, be laid before you.

The bill and amendments were referred to select committee, and ordered to be printed. The House again resolved itself into a committee of the whole on the bill preferring the mode of deciding disputed titles of President and Vice President, Mr. Rutledge in the chair, and Mr. Marshall's amendment being under consideration: Mr. Randolph moved to amend the bill by striking out that part which directs the Grand Committee to be chosen by ballot, and inserting that they shall be chosen by lot. The messages of the executive rung with the applause of his own measures and the deluded democrats all thought this was the happy result of Mr. Jefferson's administration. The vessel of state conducted through the perilous storms of European politics had reached the port in safety, when he was placed at the helm to guide it, and he was foolish enough to think that he was entitled to the credit. But now after the lapse of five years, we would call the attention of every serious and thinking friend of his country to a survey of our public affairs. It is a sad reverse. Instead of gaining respectability with the increase of our physical strength, our government has become the sport of diplomatic insolence. Our treasury has been exhausted in the purchase of a country whose limits are undefined and which will probably cost us as much again to secure it. The necessity of an efficient navy which had been foreseen and provided for by the federal rulers, is now acknowledged and the money of the nation must be squandered to supply the want of the shipping which had been disposed of merely to uphold a ridiculous boast of economy.

Boston, OCT. 6. West-India and Southern Storms. Since our last, we have received the following particulars: In the gale at St. Thomas, from 4th to 5th Sept., a fleet of vessels, principally Americans, destroyed; and in some places, lay three deep! An eastern schooner laden with lumber, upset, one man killed, number wounded. Schr Hiram, Bacon, of Barnstable, for Boston, was safe, and no damage; the Fair Trader, Crawford, of Boston, had been ashore, but got off. In Martinique, out of 12 sail at that place, all but 5 had been lost. A heavy gale has been experienced at New Providence; but no material damage is said to have been done. The gale was felt at Jacmel; but no very great damage done. At St. Croix, no material damage was done. At St. Pierres, Martinique, it is said all the vessels in the road, except 5, were totally lost. At St. Kitts, St. Barts, St. Eustatia and Nevis, most of the vessels are reported to have been lost. From Curacao and St. Vincents, we have no accounts of damage, although there have been arrivals at New-York, which left those places September 5-6. At Guadaloupe, it is stated that the shipping suffered very much, as well as at Tortola, where it is mentioned that only 4 escaped out of 40.

Weymouth. Tuesday, April 24, 1804. NEWS EXPECTED. Accounts from France to the 20th, and from England to the 24th March, may be expected in the course of a few days; vessels sailing from those places, at the period mentioned, having been spoken with by some of the late arrivals at this port. One of the vessels spoken is the Mars bound from Liverpool to New-York; the other the Eagle, from Bordeaux for Baltimore. They have probably both arrived. From the EAST-INDIES. Capt. Myrick, from Batavia, in the ship Indus, informs, that a French squadron of one 74, two frigates, and the corvette Berceau, [probably, that commanded by admiral Linois] sailed from Batavia the 8th December—which, previous to the arrival of the Indus, had destroyed the English pepper magazines at Bencoolen, (on the island of Sumatra,) to the amount, it was said, of from 18 to 20,000 piculs. And that the same squadron had captured an English ship at Bencoolen, with a valuable cargo of Calcutta and Madras goods, and sent her to the Isle of France. Accounts from the coast of Africa state, that the Isle of Goree had been assaulted and captured by a French national vessel, and privateers from Cayenne.

April 20, four arrived at Cadiz— the fleet of the Portuguese (from 18 to 24 gun, and, from 100 to 115 in all). Orders had been received from the French government by the Spanish consul at Cadiz, to take possession of all captured American property; which was complied with. The king of Spain has given to the French 12 sail of the line, ready for sea, to be dis armed and manned by Frenchmen. Six thousand French troops were on their march for Cadiz to protect the place; and the French and Spanish fleet, from Brest, were escorted to Cadiz, where 5 sail of the line from Ferrol and two frigates from Brest had arrived, the latter having on board officers and men for the above fleet. Fourteen more ships of war were daily expected from the Me diterranean. Letters from the American consul at Ma laga, and the consul at Algiers, mention, that eleven sail of American vessels had been cap tured by the Tripolitan cruisers—and that no American vessels were permitted to sail from the Mediterranean without a convoy.

The total suspension of operations upon the canal that must follow the recent failure to obtain a further subscription from the State of Maryland renders it certain, even if there should be everything done by that State next year that can be asked for by the company, that the canal will not be completed to Cumberland in less than four years from this time. It is a very easy matter to draw the line on which fair and legitimate propositions may be made, on which rightful opinions may be held, and on which full discussion may be had. It was not always wise, but it was never criminal to express a wish for peace, to urge the government to make every effort to commence negotiations for peace. This was not always wise, because, up to a very late period the enemy had shown no inclination whatever to listen to any terms, except the humiliation of an abject submission. Neither the Federal Government nor the Yankee people had given promise of any inclination for other terms. Until a late period the fortunes of the war varied; and though the true brave, patriot spirit looked assuredly for a final success, it was obliged to nerve itself for the endurance of much trial and danger, in order to its achievement. Last summer and fall, when the peace cry in North Carolina was most noisy, was a most inopportune and inappropriate period for such demonstration. Then, the balance of success was with the north. Disaster had settled heavily upon us, and the cry for peace in such a time, was like the cry of "enough" by the beaten pugilist when he gives up the fight.

Selling Literary and Political Editors, It was an old and favorite maxim of a celebrated diplomatist, who had studied human nature under very advantageous circumstances, "that every man was to be bought, if you did but know his price." In making this assertion, he always used to say that he did not simply mean, "a price in money," but that if a man in power could find out the ruling desire of any individual, you could purchase him by gratifying that ruling passion. It was always, however, presumed in this idea, that the person to be purchased was to receive the price himself; but it has been reserved for the present day, to sell literary and political talent, openly in the market, as the slave dealers do the negroes in the south, or the native princes, their captives taken on the coast of Africa. From the Canandaigua Repository. “The tables turner!"—A law in force in the territory of Michigan, provides for the sale, at public auction, of all idle and dissolute persons, on whom costs of prosecution may have accrued. A white man was, under this act, lately offered "to the highest bidder," at Detroit, in pursuance of the direction of the court before whom he had been examined. In the crowd assembled to witness the scene, appeared a sturdy negro, in the character of a purchaser, who actually bid off the property for which he paid one dollar. After hearing from the auctioneer, "yours sir," the negro walked up to his slave with all the majesty of a planter (judge Washington could not have done it better) and after bestowing several opprobrious epithets upon the trembling vassal, he concluded in a firm and impressive tone "follow your master," and moved off the ground, the purchased animal obeying him!—Thus far the black man had successfully imitated what is often seen in the southern states; but, as if disdaining to follow an example farther than the rules of justice permit, he took his victim on board the steamboat then lying off the wharf, and having safely conveyed him out of the territory, he gave him both the price of his passage, and his native freedom.

I would advise every farmer not to be too ambitious of a numerous herd of cattle, or stock of sheep; nor to keep more of either than he can keep in a thriving state. If he owns two pair of steers, or two yoke of oxen, and cannot keep their furies loose and hair slick, he must sell one. If he has ten cows, and makes small cheese, let him sell two; if that does not enlarge his cheese, let him sell two more. If his sheep be feeble, and cast their wool, let him examine his flock; if it consists of fifty, let him immediately sell ten at least. From his flock let him annually select the oldest, and the weakest of the young, and either sell them at a fair price, or feed them himself for market. With us, sheep of more than thirty in a flock, seldom answer well. Of breeds of sheep I say nothing.
